historical_timeline.summary: Sentenced to life imprisonment after the Rivonia Trial.
Prostate surgery for an enlarged gland while imprisoned.
Taken to hospital and diagnosed with tuberculosis.
Inaugurated as president of South Africa.
A raised PSA level is found on routine monitoring; a later biopsy shows microscopic prostate cancer.
Diagnosis announced; a seven-week course of curative radiotherapy begins after hormonal treatment.
His office announces that radiation treatment will continue after a review of the options.
Announces that his doctors have cleared him of prostate cancer.
Died at his home in Johannesburg.

claims.statement: Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela was born in Mvezo, in the Eastern Cape, on 18 July 1918.

Mandela was convicted with seven co-accused in the Rivonia Trial on 11 June 1964 and sentenced to life imprisonment the next day. He was held on Robben Island, moved to Pollsmoor Prison on 31 March 1982 and to Victor Verster Prison near Paarl on 7 December 1988, and was released from Victor Verster on 11 February 1990.
In 1985 Mandela had prostate surgery while imprisoned. His urologist said in July 2001 that the gland had been enlarged and was causing a urinary blockage, and that part of it was removed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: An operation for benign prostatic enlargement long before the cancer; the type of operation was not made public. Reports differ on the year and on how much of the gland was removed.

source_links.locator: Urologist's account of the earlier operation
Gives the operation as 1990 and says most of the gland was removed

claims.statement: Mandela was taken to hospital on 12 August 1988 and diagnosed with tuberculosis; public reports describe it as early tuberculosis, treated at the Constantiaberg Medi-clinic, after which he was moved to Victor Verster Prison.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Pulmonary tuberculosis treated in the past; recorded as personal history.

claims.statement: His doctors said publicly in 2001 that he had been monitored regularly with the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test, that a slight rise in the PSA led to a biopsy of the prostate, and that the biopsy confirmed microscopic cancer within the gland. News reports said the raised blood level was first found in November 2000.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A PSA rise found on monitoring, with biopsy-proven localized prostate cancer. No PSA value, Gleason score, or stage was made public.

claims.statement: His spokeswoman said in July 2001 that the cancer was not of a high grade and should not shorten his life span. He received hormonal treatment (anti-androgens) for a while and then began a seven-week course of radiotherapy with curative intent, limited to the prostate, on July 24, 2001; no surgery or chemotherapy was needed. His urologist called it a very early cancer that should be cured.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Localized, not high-grade prostate cancer treated with hormone therapy and curative radiotherapy, as his doctors and spokeswoman described it.

claims.statement: In August 2001 his office said he would continue radiation treatment after a review of the options by two physicians, a radiotherapist, and five urologists, who considered the size and grade of the tumour, the radiological tests, and his response to hormonal treatment; his office said his general health remained good.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The treatment decision as his office announced it.

claims.statement: In 2002 Mandela announced that his doctors had cleared him of prostate cancer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded as he announced it; no later result was made public and none is used.

claims.statement: Mandela was inaugurated as South Africa's first democratically elected president on 10 May 1994 and stepped down in 1999 after one term.
Mandela died at his home in Johannesburg on 5 December 2013.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Recorded as a fact; no detail of his last years is used.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Localized prostate cancer found by a rising PSA in a fit man of 82, on the NCCN prostate guideline, the AUA/ASTRO 2022 localized prostate cancer guideline, and the CMID prostate cancer monograph: risk grouping and staging (unfavorable intermediate risk, with PSMA PET); shared decision-making among observation, radiotherapy with short-term androgen deprivation, and surgery, with life expectancy and an earlier prostate operation weighed; six months of androgen deprivation with radiotherapy, and the monitoring it needs (testosterone, bone density and vitamin D, glucose and lipids, blood pressure, hot flashes, mood, and cognition); urinary and bowel effects of radiotherapy; and PSA surveillance after radiotherapy with the Phoenix definition of recurrence. His doctors' public account, a slight PSA rise on monitoring, a biopsy, hormone therapy, and a seven-week course of curative radiotherapy, frames the episode.

documentation.chief_complaint: Five-week follow-up after the prostate cancer diagnosis; staging result; radiation oncology seen today

hpi.narrative: Mr. Mandela returns five weeks after his first visit. The PSMA PET/CT two weeks ago showed uptake only in the prostate, with no spread to lymph nodes or bone. He had his DXA scan this morning and then saw Dr. van Zyl of radiation oncology, who went through observation, radiotherapy with short-term androgen deprivation, and surgery with him. He chose radiotherapy to the prostate with six months of androgen deprivation. He starts bicalutamide today and will have his first leuprolide injection at the radiation oncology clinic in one week. Before starting, he was told the expected effects of androgen deprivation (hot flashes, tiredness, loss of libido and erections, weight gain, bone loss, and changes in mood or memory) and how they are monitored. His urinary symptoms are unchanged and mild. He has no bone pain, weight loss, or breathlessness. He starts vitamin D today for the low level found at the first visit.

documentation.chief_complaint: Three-month follow-up on androgen deprivation, ten days before radiotherapy

hpi.narrative: Mr. Mandela returns three months after his last visit, twelve weeks after his first leuprolide injection. He completed four weeks of bicalutamide. Hot flashes continue three or four times a week and are mild; his energy is a little lower in the afternoons, and he still walks every morning. His weight is up 1.2 kg since starting treatment. He has had no breast tenderness, chest pain, breathlessness, or leg swelling, and his mood and memory are unchanged. Fiducial markers were placed and the planning scans done a week ago, without complications. Radiotherapy starts in ten days. Urinary symptoms are unchanged. The audiology test after his wellness visit showed mild high-frequency hearing loss on the left, and he is thinking about a hearing aid. He takes vitamin D every day.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Mandela returns six weeks after finishing 37 fractions of radiotherapy, which he completed without a break. In the fourth week he developed urinary frequency, a weaker stream, and getting up twice a night, and radiation oncology started tamsulosin 0.4 mg in the evening; these symptoms are now improving, and he has had no burning, blood in the urine, or retention, and no dizziness on standing. In the last weeks of treatment his bowels became looser, two or three times a day with some urgency, and they are now settling to once or twice a day, with no bleeding. Asked about his bowels before treatment, he says they were regular, about once a day, as recorded at his wellness visit. His second leuprolide depot ran out about three weeks ago; hot flashes are fewer, and the tiredness he had during radiotherapy is lifting. His mood is good. He has resumed his morning walks.

referral.question: Man of 82 with newly diagnosed prostate adenocarcinoma, Grade Group 3, PSA 6.4 ng/mL, cT1c, NCCN unfavorable intermediate risk, found after a rising PSA on monitoring. Please advise on curative treatment, including radiotherapy with short-term androgen deprivation, and whether observation is reasonable at his age
referral.urgency: Routine, within four to six weeks
referral.pertinent_history: Fit and independent; walks every morning. Decades ago he had an operation that removed part of the prostate for benign enlargement with urinary blockage. Treated tuberculosis in the past, with no symptoms since. A rise in PSA on routine monitoring led to a multiparametric MRI (28 mL gland with a resection defect; 9 mm PI-RADS 4 lesion in the left peripheral zone; no extraprostatic extension) and an MRI-ultrasound fusion transperineal biopsy: Gleason 4+3 in 1 of 2 targeted cores (30 percent) and Gleason 3+4 in 2 of 12 systematic cores; 3 of 14 cores positive. Digital rectal examination: smooth, no nodule. PSA 6.4 ng/mL, testosterone 412 ng/dL, hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, eGFR 69, alkaline phosphatase 74 U/L, A1c 5.5 percent, LDL 112 mg/dL, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 26 ng/mL. IPSS 7. PHQ-9 score 4. No regular medicines. PSMA PET/CT ordered; DXA booked for the day of the consultation
questions: Do you agree with the risk group, and is staging complete with the PSMA PET/CT?
What are his curative options at 82, and is observation a reasonable choice?
If radiotherapy is chosen, should androgen deprivation be added, for how long, and how should it start?
Does his earlier prostate operation change the choice of technique or his risk of urinary side effects?
What monitoring is needed during and after treatment, including PSA follow-up, and which parts should primary care manage?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Mandela is seen at the request of Dr. Mokoena for newly diagnosed prostate cancer. A rise in PSA on routine monitoring led to an MRI and a targeted biopsy, which showed Grade Group 3 adenocarcinoma in 3 of 14 cores. He has mild urinary frequency, with an IPSS of 7, and no bone pain, weight loss, or blood in the urine. Decades ago part of his prostate was removed for benign enlargement. He had tuberculosis in the past, treated, with no symptoms since. He is independent, walks every morning, and keeps a full schedule of work and travel. He wants to understand all the options before deciding
consultant_note.data_reviewed: MRI prostate report and images, biopsy pathology, the first-visit PSA, testosterone, blood count, chemistry, A1c, lipids, and 25-hydroxyvitamin D, the PSMA PET/CT from two weeks ago (uptake confined to the left peripheral zone; no nodal, bone, or visceral disease), and the DXA scan from this morning (femoral neck T-score -1.4, lumbar spine -0.6)

assessment.display: Prostate adenocarcinoma, cT1c N0 M0, Grade Group 3, PSA 6.4 ng/mL, NCCN unfavorable intermediate risk
assessment.assessment: I agree with the risk group: Grade Group 3 alone places him in the unfavorable intermediate group. The PSMA PET/CT shows no nodal or distant disease, so staging is complete. He is fit, and his life expectancy is estimated at about ten years, so curative treatment is reasonable. Observation, with treatment only if symptoms develop, is also a reasonable choice at his age and was discussed. Active surveillance is not recommended for Grade Group 3 disease. Radical prostatectomy is not advised at his age and after his earlier prostate operation, which raises the risk of incontinence. Brachytherapy is not advised because of the resection defect. The recommended option is external beam radiotherapy to the prostate with four to six months of androgen deprivation

In unfavorable intermediate-risk disease, adding four to six months of androgen deprivation to radiotherapy improves cancer control. Starting it about three months before radiotherapy also shrinks the gland. A GnRH agonist with an anti-androgen for the first weeks blocks the testosterone flare. The main effects to monitor are hot flashes, fatigue, sexual effects, weight gain, bone loss, metabolic and cardiovascular risk, and changes in mood or memory

assessment.display: Earlier prostate operation and urinary function
assessment.assessment: The resection defect does not prevent external beam radiotherapy, but it slightly raises the risk of urinary irritation and, rarely, of a urethral stricture. Mild baseline symptoms (IPSS 7) are favorable. Moderate hypofractionation (60 Gy in 20 fractions or 70 Gy in 28) and conventional fractionation (74 to 80 Gy in 2 Gy fractions) give similar cancer control; after discussion of the shorter course and the lower dose per fraction, conventional fractionation of 74 Gy in 37 fractions was chosen
Low bone mass at the femoral neck with mild vitamin D insufficiency. Ten-year hip fracture risk is below 3 percent, so no bone drug is needed for a six-month course

recommendations: External beam radiotherapy to the prostate and proximal seminal vesicles, 74 Gy in 37 daily fractions with intensity modulation and daily image guidance on fiducial markers; no pelvic nodal radiation

Androgen deprivation for six months: bicalutamide 50 mg daily for four weeks starting today, leuprolide 22.5 mg intramuscularly in one week at this clinic and a second dose twelve weeks later, with radiotherapy starting about three months after the first injection
Fiducial markers and planning CT and MRI about two weeks before radiotherapy

During androgen deprivation: testosterone and PSA at three months, blood pressure and weight at every visit, hot flashes, fatigue, mood, and cognition reviewed at each visit, and glucose and lipids yearly
Bone health: vitamin D 1000 units daily with a recheck in three months, calcium from food, resistance exercise, and DXA every one to two years
During radiotherapy: weekly review for urinary and bowel effects; tamsulosin if urinary frequency or a weak stream develops; report blood in the urine or stool

After radiotherapy: PSA six weeks after treatment, then every six months for five years and yearly after that; recurrence is a PSA rise of 2 ng/mL above the nadir (Phoenix); a temporary PSA bounce is not recurrence
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Mokoena today. The patient chose radiotherapy with six months of androgen deprivation after hearing each option, including observation, and agrees with the plan
consultant_note.follow_up: Leuprolide injection here in one week. Fiducial markers and planning in about twelve weeks. Weekly review during radiotherapy, then radiation oncology three months after treatment and every six months. Primary care manages the androgen deprivation monitoring, bone health, blood pressure, distress screening, and PSA surveillance between reviews
